title: 1:1 — Sarah & Marcus
description: Fortnightly one-to-one. Team capacity and the config review trade-off.
transcript: Long. The incident ate most of it.
I saw. Are you okay? You were online very late on Tuesday.
I'm fine. It wasn't the incident that kept me up, it was writing the postmortem afterwards.
It is when you have to be honest about the cause.
The cause was that we let anyone change production config without review. That's not a mistake someone made, that's a process we chose not to build.
It's uncomfortable to write down because it means the incident was predictable.
For what it's worth, I'd rather read that postmortem than one that blames a person.
That's why I wrote it that way. But I want to make sure the fix actually happens, otherwise the honesty is decorative.
That's fair pressure to put on me.
It's not aimed at you specifically.
No, but it lands with me, and it should. Let's talk about what it costs.
Two engineer-weeks. Realistically that's James, because he knows the deployment path best.
James is also the person unblocking mobile onboarding.
Which is the whole problem. He's the constraint on both.
Is that a bus-factor issue we should be fixing separately?
Yes, honestly. There's a lot in his head that isn't written down.
Okay, park that — I want to come back to it. First: which one goes first?
The config work protects us from a future incident. The onboarding work is already two weeks late and has been promised to the board twice.
That's a more political answer than I expected from you.
It's not political, it's about credibility. If we slip onboarding again nobody believes our next estimate, including the config estimate.
That's a good argument. I withdraw the accusation.
So James does onboarding first, then config. What's the exposure in the gap?
Roughly three weeks where a bad config change can still take out production.
Can we reduce that without building the whole thing?
Partly. I could put a two-person rule on the rate limit config specifically — just that one file — in about a day.
That covers the failure mode we actually hit.
It covers the one we hit twice, yes. It doesn't cover the general case.
I'll take a day of work that covers the thing that's actually happened twice.
Then I'll do that this week.
Good. Now — back to the bus factor.
I've been avoiding this conversation, if I'm honest.
Because the answer is that we need to hire, and I know what the hiring conversation looks like right now.
It's not as closed as you think. What would you ask for?
One backend engineer. Not senior necessarily — someone who can absorb the deployment knowledge and pair with James for a quarter.
That's a more modest ask than I expected.
A second senior wouldn't help. The problem isn't capability, it's that one person holds all the context.
Write that up. Half a page, and make the bus-factor argument explicitly — not 'we're busy', which is what every req says.
Before the end of next week.
Good. I'd rather take it to Raj with a specific risk attached than a general request for headcount.
One thing, and it's a bit awkward.
In the roadmap meeting you asked me for a one-pager by Friday, and then in the same meeting Priya got asked for a scope by Thursday and James got reassigned.
It felt like a lot of commitments made quickly without checking what was already in flight.
That's a completely fair criticism and I'd rather hear it now than not at all.
I wasn't sure whether to raise it.
Always raise it. What would you have preferred?
Just — 'what does that displace?' before agreeing a date. Half the time the answer is 'nothing' and it costs ten seconds.
That's easy to do and I'll do it. Thank you.
Was there anything from my side you wanted?
Not really. I'd like to know earlier when board dates move, because that's usually what compresses everything.
That's reasonable. I'll forward the calendar invite rather than mentioning it in passing.
Okay. Same time in two weeks?

summary.overview: Marcus's postmortem attributes the rate-limit incident to an absent process rather than an individual error, and he pressed for the fix to be funded rather than acknowledged. He argued onboarding should still go first — not politically, but because a third slip would discredit every subsequent estimate including the config one — and proposed a one-day two-person rule on the rate-limit config to cover the interim. The underlying issue is that James is the single constraint on both workstreams, so Marcus will write a headcount request framed explicitly as bus-factor risk. Marcus also raised that commitments in the roadmap meeting were agreed without checking what they displaced.
summary.gist: Onboarding first, one-day stopgap on config, and a bus-factor headcount case to write up.

outline.title: Feedback on how commitments were made

bullets: Root cause written as a process gap, not human error — the incident was predictable.
Marcus wants the fix funded, otherwise the candour in the postmortem is decorative.
Config work prevents a future incident; onboarding is already two weeks late and promised to the board twice.
A third slip would discredit every later estimate, including the config one.
Roughly three weeks of exposure while onboarding takes priority.
One day of work adds a two-person rule to the rate-limit config specifically — covers the failure that has now happened twice, not the general case.
James is the sole constraint on both workstreams; much of the deployment knowledge is undocumented.
Ask is one mid-level backend engineer to pair and absorb context — not a second senior.
To be written up as a specific risk rather than a general capacity request.

notes.chapter: Feedback on how commitments were made
bullets: Several dates were agreed in one meeting without checking what they displaced.
Agreed remedy: ask 'what does that displace?' before accepting a date.
Board date changes to be forwarded as calendar invites rather than mentioned in passing.

Write the half-page headcount case framed as bus-factor risk
Forward board calendar invites rather than mentioning date changes in passing
